# HyperFund/HyperVerse: Investigation of the Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The available evidence describes HyperFund as an alleged global crypto investment-fraud network that combined four mutually reinforcing components: unusually high “passive” returns, multi-level recruitment incentives, repeated rebranding, and credibility-building through public promoters and apparently fabricated corporate leadership.

The scheme was initially presented as HyperFund, launched in June 2020 by the purported HyperTech Group. It later became HyperVerse in late 2021 and HyperNation in 2022. Investors were allegedly offered membership packages that promised daily returns of approximately 0.5% to 1%, potentially doubling or tripling their initial investment. Promotional materials attributed those returns partly to large-scale cryptocurrency mining, although the SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund had no such mining operations and that founder Sam Lee later acknowledged that the relevant mining activity had ended before HyperFund launched ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The recruitment structure allegedly resembled both a Ponzi scheme and a pyramid or multi-level marketing scheme. Investors were encouraged to remain “passive,” but were also offered additional rewards for recruiting participants into downlines extending as many as 20 levels. According to the SEC’s allegations, the network lacked sufficient legitimate revenue and used new investor deposits to facilitate withdrawals by earlier participants ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Public promoters played a central role in converting the scheme’s abstract claims into a persuasive investment narrative. Brenda Chunga, known online as “Bitcoin Beautee,” allegedly became one of HyperFund’s leading U.S. promoters, reaching the highest promoter level after generating at least $5 million in referred “sales.” The SEC alleges that she received approximately $3.7 million from platform withdrawals and direct transactions with investors ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The rebranding strategy appears to have preserved continuity while changing the project’s narrative. HyperFund was marketed as a decentralized-finance ecosystem, HyperVerse as a metaverse, and HyperNation as a blockchain-based decentralized society. The SEC alleges that investors were moved between the iterations while withdrawal problems continued. At the same time, HyperVerse introduced “Steven Reece Lewis” as its chief executive officer. The Guardian reported that universities, corporate registries, Adobe, Goldman Sachs, and the SEC had no records supporting his claimed education or career. The SEC complaint went further, alleging that “Steven Reece Lewis” was a paid actor portraying a fabricated character ([The Guardian, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist); [SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

My assessment is that the evidence supports a coherent alleged fraud architecture rather than a collection of isolated misrepresentations: promised returns attracted capital; referral rewards accelerated recruitment; public promoters supplied social proof; rebranding helped maintain engagement after operational problems emerged; and the questionable CEO persona supplied an additional layer of apparent legitimacy. However, because several key facts remain allegations in a civil complaint or criminal charging documents, they should not be treated as final judicial findings unless confirmed by adjudication.

## Scope and source assessment

This report relies only on the four distinct sources supplied in the case materials:

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary character | Principal value |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | CNBC report, January 29, 2024 | Reputable secondary reporting based on DOJ and SEC actions | Concise chronology, defendants, criminal charges, alleged losses |
| S2 | U.S. Department of Justice, HyperFund case page | Official government case record | Case numbers, charges, plea status, later procedural updates |
| S3 | The Guardian, January 4, 2024 | Investigative secondary reporting | Investigation into “Steven Reece Lewis,” celebrity endorsements, investor experience |
| S4 | SEC civil complaint, filed January 29, 2024 | Primary legal pleading; allegations, not findings | Detailed mechanics, money flows, promotional claims, rebranding, alleged false representations |

The SEC complaint and DOJ materials are the most authoritative sources for the allegations and procedural posture. The Guardian provides independent reporting that is particularly relevant to the alleged CEO identity. CNBC usefully summarizes the government actions but is less detailed than the underlying pleadings.

## How the alleged investment model worked

### Membership packages and promised returns

According to the SEC complaint, investors purchased HyperFund “memberships” using Tether, or USDT. Examples included membership levels of $300, $500, $1,000, and $10,000. The platform represented the purchased value internally as “HyperUnits,” with a $300 membership corresponding to 300 HyperUnits ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The memberships allegedly promised several benefits:

1. Access to a crypto-asset educational platform.
2. Discounted access to future crypto projects or initial coin offerings.
3. Automatic daily “rewards.”
4. Additional rewards for recruitment and organizational growth.

The most important financial promise was a daily passive return of approximately 0.5% to 1%, allegedly continuing until the investor’s original amount had doubled or tripled. The SEC complaint states that HyperFund presented the possibility of tripling the original investment in 600 days. CNBC similarly reported that investors were told they could receive daily returns until their initial investment doubled or tripled through supposed crypto-mining revenue ([CNBC, 2024](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

These promised returns were economically extraordinary. Even without compounding, a return of 0.5% per day would imply 182.5% annually; a 1% daily return would imply 365% annually. The materials portrayed these returns as passive, requiring no conventional employment or business activity by the investor. Chunga allegedly told prospective investors that their money would “do all of the work” without them needing to get out of bed ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

### Recruitment and downline incentives

The passive-return narrative was paired with a recruitment system. HyperFund allegedly offered “Community Rewards,” “VIP Rewards,” and “Global Rewards.” Community Rewards were described as compensation tied to the value of an investor’s downline, potentially extending through 20 levels. VIP status could generate additional daily rewards when an investor’s organization reached specified sales thresholds. Global Rewards allegedly distributed a percentage of company sales among top promoters ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

This structure served two functions. First, it created an additional reason for participants to recruit rather than simply hold a membership. Second, it generated a network of promoters who had a personal financial incentive to repeat the company’s claims. The alleged scheme therefore did not rely solely on formal advertising. It delegated persuasion to participants whose compensation depended on bringing in new capital.

The Guardian independently described a similar structure: members were paid referral commissions based on recruitment, with further commissions based on recruits recruiting others, down to 20 levels ([The Guardian, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

## The alleged Ponzi and pyramid mechanics

The SEC characterizes HyperFund as both a pyramid scheme and a Ponzi scheme. The distinction matters:

- The alleged **pyramid component** concerned recruitment-based rewards and downline commissions.
- The alleged **Ponzi component** concerned the use of new investor funds to satisfy withdrawal obligations or create the appearance of successful returns.

The SEC alleges that HyperFund had no meaningful source of revenue apart from money received from investors. It further alleges that the promised mining operations did not exist and that withdrawals were funded by new investor deposits ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The withdrawal mechanism allegedly introduced additional friction. Investors could not simply redeem HyperUnits for dollars. Instead, they had to convert them into Molecular Future, or MOF, transfer the MOF to the HOO Exchange, convert it into another crypto asset, and then attempt to exchange that asset for fiat currency. The complaint alleges that although HyperUnits were displayed at a nominal value of $1 when deposited, the conversion value on withdrawal was not fixed. By September 2023, the SEC reported that MOF was quoted at approximately $0.00001949, although the complaint also states that it did not appear to be actively traded ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

This mechanism could make the platform appear to recognize investor balances while making actual cash extraction difficult. It also created opportunities to explain failed withdrawals as technical or market problems rather than as evidence of insolvency.

## Public promoters and social proof

### Brenda Chunga

Brenda Chunga was allegedly one of HyperFund’s most prominent U.S. promoters. The SEC alleges that she joined in September 2020, began hosting online presentations, and became one of only six “corporate” presenters and one of only two in the United States ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Within approximately six months, she allegedly reached “VIP 5 STAR,” the highest promoter level, requiring at least $5 million in referred investments. She allegedly withdrew approximately $2.5 million from the platform and received an additional approximately $1.1 million directly from investors, for total receipts of about $3.7 million. The SEC alleges that these funds supported luxury purchases and conspicuous displays of wealth used to recruit additional investors ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

This alleged activity illustrates a classic social-proof mechanism. Visible consumption was not merely personal spending; according to the complaint, it functioned as promotional evidence. Wealth was presented as proof that the system worked, which could encourage additional investment even when the underlying revenue claims were unsupported.

Chunga pleaded guilty in the criminal case to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud, according to the DOJ and CNBC. The DOJ page identifies her case as *United States v. Brenda Chunga*, docket number 24-CR-1 ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [CNBC, 2024](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html)).

### Sam Lee and founder credibility

Sam Lee, also identified as Xue Samuel Lee, was presented in promotional materials as a founder or chairman associated with HyperTech and HyperFund. The SEC alleges that his background, media appearances, and links to Blockchain Global were used to create credibility. Promotional materials also allegedly represented that the HyperTech Group was connected to DigitalX and IBM, claims that the SEC complaint says were false or misleading ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The complaint further alleges that Lee knew, or recklessly disregarded, that promoters were describing large-scale crypto-mining operations that did not exist. In a recorded 2023 call, Lee allegedly stated that the group had stopped mining in 2019 and no longer owned mining machines because mining was not profitable ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Lee was criminally charged with conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. He was also named in the SEC’s civil action. These remain charges and allegations rather than a final determination of criminal liability ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

## Rebranding as a continuity strategy

The project allegedly changed names several times:

| Brand | Approximate period | Public narrative described in the evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| HyperCapital | Before June 2020 | Earlier related multi-level marketing project |
| HyperFund | June 2020 onward | Decentralized-finance ecosystem and crypto rewards |
| HyperVerse | Late 2021 | Metaverse, virtual world, and native token |
| HyperNation | May 2022 | Blockchain-based decentralized society or government |

The SEC alleges that HyperFund became HyperVerse around December 2021 and HyperNation around May 2022. The changes altered the language and imagery surrounding the project while retaining the membership and reward concepts. HyperVerse introduced a virtual-world narrative, while HyperNation used a political and ideological narrative involving decentralization, inequality, and a universal basic income ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [The Guardian, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

The evidence indicates that rebranding may have served as a reputational reset. Rather than confronting the failure of one investment product, promoters could present a successor project with new terminology and new aspirational goals. The SEC alleges that investors were moved from HyperFund to HyperVerse and later encouraged to transition to HyperNation, even as withdrawal difficulties persisted ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

## The questionable CEO persona

The introduction of “Steven Reece Lewis” was a particularly important credibility device. During the December 2021 HyperVerse launch, he was presented as CEO and described as having attended the University of Leeds and the University of Cambridge, worked at Goldman Sachs, sold a web-development company to Adobe, and founded an information-technology startup ([The Guardian, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

The Guardian reported that it could not verify these credentials. It stated that neither university had a record of him, that Companies House and SEC searches found no relevant records, that Adobe had no public record of acquiring a company owned by him, and that Goldman Sachs could not locate evidence that he had worked there ([The Guardian, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

The SEC complaint alleges more directly that the person presented as Lewis was a paid actor portraying a fabricated character and was not HyperVerse’s actual CEO. The complaint states that the actor worked as a television presenter in Bangkok and that Lee knew, or was reckless in not knowing, that the presentation was false ([SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Celebrity videos reinforced the launch. The Guardian reported that Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass released supportive messages. The article noted that these individuals were available through Cameo and that there was no suggestion they understood HyperVerse’s business model or knew of the alleged investment fraud ([The Guardian, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

## Collapse, withdrawal restrictions, and scale

The sources differ somewhat in describing the timing of withdrawal restrictions:

- CNBC reported the DOJ allegation that withdrawals began to be blocked in July 2021.
- The SEC complaint states that investors experienced increasing withdrawal difficulties in November or December 2021, were generally unable to withdraw by February or March 2022, and could not redeem investments after November 2022.
- The SEC complaint separately states that the HOO Exchange suspended withdrawals in June 2022 and ultimately stopped functioning by November 2022 ([CNBC, 2024](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The apparent discrepancy may reflect different definitions of “blocking withdrawals”—for example, initial restrictions, increasingly limited withdrawals, or the final inability to redeem funds. It should not be resolved by selecting one date without qualification.

The reported scale also varies. CNBC and the DOJ describe an alleged $1.89 billion or approximately $1.9 billion criminal fraud scheme. The SEC complaint states that HyperFund raised more than $1.7 billion worldwide. These figures may reflect different calculations, periods, or evidentiary bases, but the sources do not provide enough information to reconcile them definitively ([CNBC, 2024](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [SEC complaint, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

## Overall assessment

The evidence supports the following assessment: HyperFund/HyperVerse allegedly operated through an integrated persuasion-and-finance system. The promised returns created urgency and apparent inevitability; recruitment rewards turned investors into distributors; public promoters supplied personal testimonials and visible wealth; founder biographies and corporate affiliations supplied institutional legitimacy; rebranding preserved the community’s expectations after operational problems; and the questionable CEO persona added a polished executive face to the HyperVerse transition.

The central alleged contradiction was between the public explanation for returns—large-scale crypto mining and legitimate business revenue—and the SEC’s allegation that the platform had no such revenue and depended on new investor funds. The alleged use of a fabricated CEO and disputed corporate credentials further suggests that image management was not incidental but part of the recruitment architecture.

Nevertheless, the report must distinguish allegations from adjudicated facts. Chunga’s guilty plea is a confirmed procedural event, while the SEC’s descriptions of Lee’s intent, the fabricated CEO, the absence of mining operations, and the full operation of the scheme remain allegations in the supplied legal record unless otherwise established by a court.

## References

The Guardian. (2024, January 4). *Chief executive of collapsed crypto fund HyperVerse does not appear to exist*. [The Guardian website](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)
